title: Git's Mental Model
summary: Git stores snapshots in a content-addressed DAG, not diffs against a previous version. Get this model right and branches, merges, and recovery all stop feeling like magic.

slides.markdown:
Most engineers use git for years while picturing it wrong: as a chain of diffs, each commit a patch on top of the last. That model breaks the moment you try to explain what a branch actually is, or why a rebase can rewrite history without touching a single file on disk.

The real model is simpler and more powerful: git is a **content-addressed database of snapshots**. Every commit is a complete picture of your project at that moment, not an instruction for how to get there from the last one. Branches and tags are just labels pointing into that database.

Every other git feature — merging, rebasing, `bisect`, the reflog — is built on this one idea. Get it solid here and the rest of the toolchain stops being a list of memorized commands.

slides.subTitle: Why git differs from CVS/SVN
slides.markdown:
Older version control systems (CVS, Subversion) store each file as a **base version plus a chain of diffs**. To reconstruct file X at revision 40, the tool replays 40 patches in order. That's why old-style history can be slow to check out and fragile — corrupt one diff in the chain and everything after it is unreadable.

Git stores something different: at every commit, it saves the **complete tree of every file's content** as it existed at that moment. If a file didn't change between two commits, both commits simply point at the same stored blob — no diff, no chain, just a shared reference.

Diffs still show up constantly (`git diff`, PR reviews) but they're **computed on demand** by comparing two snapshots. They are a view onto the data, not the storage format. This is also why checking out any commit, however old, is equally fast — there's no chain to replay, just a hash to look up.

slides.subTitle: Commits, parents, branches, and tags as pointers
slides.markdown:
Every commit stores the hash of its **parent commit** (or parents, for a merge). Follow those parent links backward and you get a directed acyclic graph (DAG) — acyclic because a commit can never point back to something that came after it.

A **branch** is nothing more than a movable pointer to one commit in that graph — a sticky note that says "this is where `main` currently is," which git slides forward automatically every time you commit while that branch is checked out. A **tag** is the same idea but frozen: it doesn't move when you commit.

This reframes almost every git operation as graph manipulation: branching is adding a new sticky note, merging is adding a commit with two parents, rebasing is moving a sticky note's commits onto a different point in the graph. None of it touches file contents directly — it's all pointer and graph arithmetic underneath.

![Directed acyclic graph of commits with main and feature branch pointers, a merge commit, and a fixed tag](assets/commit-dag-branches.svg)

slides.subTitle: Working directory, staging area, HEAD
slides.markdown:
Every git command manipulates one of three trees, and knowing which one explains most "why did that happen" confusion:

- **Working directory** — the actual files on disk, exactly what your editor and IDE see. Can hold anything, tracked or not.
- **Staging area (the index)** — a snapshot-in-progress. `git add` copies a file's current content here. This is the tree that `git commit` actually commits.
- **HEAD (the repo)** — the last commit on your current branch, i.e. the last snapshot git has permanently recorded.

The staging area is the feature people underuse: it means a commit is never "whatever the files currently look like" — it's whatever you explicitly staged, which can be a subset of your changes (`git add -p` to stage half a file's edits). This is also why `git status` shows two separate change lists: "changes not staged" (working dir vs index) and "changes to be committed" (index vs HEAD).

slides.subTitle: Untracked to staged to committed
slides.markdown:
A new file walks through a small, fixed set of states, and every git command that touches files is really just a transition between them:

**Untracked** (git has never seen this path) → `git add` → **Staged** (content is in the index, ready to commit) → `git commit` → **Committed** (content is permanently in a snapshot, tied to a commit hash).

An already-tracked file adds one more loop: after a commit, editing it moves it to **Modified** (tracked, but working dir differs from HEAD), and `git add` moves it back to Staged from there. `git restore` and `git reset` are the reverse arrows — they move a file backward through these same states without creating new commits.

![State diagram of a file moving between untracked, staged, committed, and modified](assets/file-state-lifecycle.svg)

assets.alt: State diagram of a file moving between untracked, staged, committed, and modified

slides.subTitle: Tree + parent + author + message, hashed
slides.markdown:
A commit object is small — it's mostly pointers, not file content:

- a pointer to a **tree** object (the root directory snapshot — itself a list of file names pointing at blob hashes, recursively for subdirectories)
- a pointer to its **parent commit** hash (or none, for the first commit; or two, for a merge)
- **author** and **committer** name/email/timestamp (these can differ — think `cherry-pick`, which keeps the original author but sets you as committer)
- the **commit message**

All of that gets hashed (SHA-1, historically) to produce the commit's own ID. Because the hash covers the parent pointer too, changing anything about an old commit — even just its message — changes its hash, which changes every descendant commit's hash in turn. That's the real reason a rebase or amend "rewrites history": it's not editing commits in place, it's building entirely new commit objects and moving the branch pointer to the new chain.

slides.subTitle: What "checking out a commit" means
slides.markdown:
**HEAD** is a pointer to "where you currently are." Normally it points *at a branch* (e.g. `main`), and the branch in turn points at a commit — so HEAD moves automatically whenever the branch moves.

Run `git checkout <commit-hash>` (or `git switch --detach`) instead of checking out a branch name, and HEAD points **directly at a commit**, with no branch in between. This is **detached HEAD**: you can look around, build, even test things, but if you commit here, that new commit has no branch pointing at it. Switch to another branch and it becomes unreachable — recoverable only via the reflog until garbage collection (§ Advanced Git Internals).

The fix, if you meant to keep work done in detached HEAD, is `git switch -c new-branch-name` right then — that plants a branch pointer on your current commit before you move away from it.

Four commands cover most of a normal working session:

```bash
git status                 # working dir + index state, in plain English
git add path/to/file.py    # working dir -> staging area
git commit -m "message"    # staging area -> new commit, HEAD moves
git log --oneline --graph  # walk the commit DAG from HEAD backward
```

`git status` is the single most useful debugging command in git — read it before guessing. It names untracked files, modified-but-unstaged files, and staged-and-ready files in three separate sections, which maps directly onto the three trees from earlier.

`git log --oneline --graph` is worth memorizing as a pair of flags: `--oneline` collapses each commit to one line (short hash + message), and `--graph` draws the ASCII branch/merge topology next to it, so you can see the DAG shape instead of a flat list.

All three print a diff. The difference is entirely **which two trees they compare**:

| Command | Compares | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `git diff` | working directory vs staging area | "What have I changed but not staged yet?" |
| `git diff --staged` | staging area vs HEAD | "What am I about to commit?" |
| `git show <commit>` | that commit's tree vs its parent's tree | "What did this past commit actually change?" |

A common confusion: running `git diff` right after `git add` and seeing nothing. That's correct behavior, not a bug — `git diff` only looks at working-dir-vs-index, and you just made those identical. The change is visible with `git diff --staged` instead, because now index-vs-HEAD is where the difference lives.

slides.sectionTitle: Why secrets and binaries in history are forever
slides.markdown:
Because a commit's hash chains into every descendant's hash, **you cannot delete a file from one old commit without rewriting every commit after it** (`git filter-repo` / BFG do exactly this — they rebuild the whole chain). Simply deleting the file and committing that deletion does nothing to history: the blob is still reachable from the old commit, sitting in `.git`, one `git show <old-hash>:path` away from anyone with the repo.

This makes two mistakes uniquely expensive in git, unlike in tools with centralized history:

- **Committing a secret** (API key, credential file) — rotating the credential is mandatory the moment it's pushed; deleting it later doesn't un-leak it, since anyone who already fetched has the blob.
- **Committing a large binary** (a video, a build artifact, a database dump) — it permanently bloats every future clone of the repo, because a full clone fetches the entire object database, not just the current snapshot.

The practical guard is a `.gitignore` before the first commit and a pre-commit hook that blocks known secret patterns — cheaper than any history-rewrite after the fact.

slides.sectionTitle: Content addressing as an integrity guarantee
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
Because every object's ID is a hash of its own content (and, for commits, its parent's hash too), git gets tamper detection for free: change one byte anywhere in history and every hash from that point forward changes. This is why git can safely fetch objects over an untrusted network and from untrusted mirrors — a corrupted or tampered object simply won't match the hash you asked for.

Content addressing also gives automatic deduplication: if you copy a 10 MB file to a new path unchanged, git stores **one** blob and points two tree entries at it — no extra space, no manual dedup logic.

The one asterisk staff engineers should know: git's original hash function is SHA-1, and known (expensive, engineered) collision attacks exist against plain SHA-1 — though not yet a practical *second-preimage* attack that could forge a specific existing object undetected. Git mitigates this today with a hardened SHA-1 variant, and the project has a long-running, largely backward-compatible migration path to SHA-256 for new repositories. In an interview, knowing *why* content addressing matters (integrity + dedup) is worth more than the hash algorithm trivia.
